title: Market Failure and the Role of Government

questions.question: A factory pollutes a river, shifting costs onto downstream villages. This is an example of:
questions.rationale: A cost imposed on third parties that the price does not capture is a negative externality: private cost (Rs 30,000/tonne, say) is below social cost (Rs 40,000), so the market over-produces.

questions.question: A tax set equal to the marginal external cost of an activity is called a:
questions.rationale: Pigou's remedy: tax the externality until private cost equals social cost. Output then falls to the social optimum instead of the market's too-high level.

questions.question: National defence is the textbook example of a public good because it is:
questions.rationale: One citizen's protection does not reduce another's (non-rival) and no citizen can be left unprotected (non-excludable). Free-riding then starves private provision, which is why states finance defence through taxation.

questions.question: Over-fishing in international waters is an illustration of:
questions.rationale: Fisheries are rival but non-excludable - a common resource. Each boat ignores the depletion it causes others, so effort expands until the stock collapses. Quotas, licences or property rights are the standard remedies.

questions.question: An industry where one firm can supply the entire market at lowest cost because of huge economies of scale is a:
questions.rationale: Rail tracks or electricity grids cost so much per extra customer-relevant scale that duplicating them wastes resources. The policy menu: public ownership, or regulated pricing (average-cost pricing to break even, marginal-cost pricing with subsidy).

questions.question: Akerlof's 'market for lemons' illustrates:
questions.rationale: Before the sale, only the seller knows the car's quality; buyers discount all cars, so owners of good cars withdraw, and the market unravels toward lemons. Moral hazard is the AFTER-contract problem of changed behaviour.

questions.question: An insured person driving more recklessly is an example of:
questions.rationale: Moral hazard is hidden action after the deal: insurance changes behaviour because consequences shift to the insurer. Deductibles and co-pays exist precisely to keep skin in the game.

questions.question: Education is often subsidised because it is treated as a:
options: Pure private good with no spillovers
questions.rationale: Educated citizens generate spillovers (productivity, citizenship, lower crime) that private tuition fees do not capture, so the market under-consumes it. Subsidies align private choice with social benefit.

questions.question: The Coase theorem states that private bargaining can solve an externality when:
options: Property rights are clear and transaction costs are negligible
questions.rationale: With clear rights and cheap bargaining, the parties trade to the efficient outcome regardless of who initially holds the right. In reality a million polluters and victims make transaction costs enormous, which is why legislation, not negotiation, handles smog.

questions.question: Regulatory capture refers to:
options: The regulator serving the interests of the industry it oversees
questions.rationale: Capture is a flagship case of government failure: expertise, revolving doors and lobbying bend the agency toward the regulated. It is the standing counter-argument that intervention beats market failure only when it does not replace it with a worse one.
